details:
**The Awakening (Edna Pontellier)**
Chopin's 1899 novel, her most famous work, about Edna Pontellier, a wife and mother in Creole Louisiana who awakens to her own desires and rejects the roles of wife and mother. It was condemned on publication for its frank treatment of female independence and sexuality and is now considered an early feminist classic.

**Drowning in the Gulf of Mexico**
The ending of The Awakening. After Robert Lebrun leaves her with a farewell note ("Good-by—because I love you"), Edna returns to Grand Isle, swims naked out into the Gulf of Mexico, and drowns, thinking of her childhood and of Mademoiselle Reisz as she goes.

**Robert Lebrun and Alcée Arobin**
Edna's two romantic interests in The Awakening. She falls in love with the young Robert Lebrun while vacationing at Grand Isle, but he flees to Mexico and later leaves her again. While he is away, she has an affair with the seducer Alcée Arobin and moves out of her husband Léonce's house into a small "pigeon house."

**"The Story of an Hour" (Louise Mallard)**
Chopin's very short story in which Louise Mallard, who has heart trouble, learns from her sister Josephine that her husband Brently has died in a railroad accident. Alone in her room at an open window, she sees "a long procession of years to come that would belong to her absolutely" and whispers "Free! Body and soul free!"

**"The joy that kills"**
The ending of "The Story of an Hour." Louise descends the stairs "like a goddess of Victory," but Brently Mallard walks in alive, having been far from the accident, and she dies on the spot. The doctors ironically say she died of heart disease, "of the joy that kills."

**"Désirée's Baby" (Armand Aubigny)**
A Chopin story in which Désirée, a foundling adopted by the Valmondes, marries the plantation owner Armand Aubigny, who falls in love with her "as if struck by a pistol shot." When their baby turns out to have visibly African ancestry, Armand coldly rejects her, and she carries the baby off into the bayou and disappears among the reeds and willows.

**The burning of the cradle and the letter from Armand's mother**
The twist ending of "Désirée's Baby." Armand burns Désirée's belongings, including the willow cradle, in a bonfire, and then finds a letter from his own mother thanking God that Armand will never know that "his mother... belongs to the race that is cursed with the brand of slavery." He, not Désirée, had Black ancestry.

**Mademoiselle Reisz and Adèle Ratignolle**
Two contrasting women in The Awakening. The unpleasant, solitary pianist Mademoiselle Reisz, whose playing moves Edna to tears, represents the independent artist and encourages her rebellion. Adèle Ratignolle is the ideal "mother-woman," devoted to her husband and children, who reminds Edna of her duty to her family.

**The parrot ("Allez vous-en!")**
The Awakening opens with a caged parrot at Grand Isle shrieking "Allez vous-en! Allez vous-en! Sapristi!" ("Go away! Go away! For God's sake!") as Léonce Pontellier tries to read his newspaper. The caged bird symbolizes Edna's confinement.

**"The Storm" (Calixta and Alcée)**
A Chopin story in which Calixta's husband Bobinot and their four-year-old son Bibi buy a can of shrimp at the store and wait out a storm there. Meanwhile, her former lover Alcée takes shelter at her house; after lightning strikes a tree, he asks if she remembers their time at Assumption, and they make love. The story ends, "So the storm passed and every one was happy." It was not published in Chopin's lifetime.

**"A Pair of Silk Stockings" (Mrs. Sommers)**
A Chopin story in which the poor mother Mrs. Sommers unexpectedly gets fifteen dollars, plans to spend it on her children, but instead buys herself silk stockings, gloves, magazines, a fine lunch, and a theater ticket. On the cable car home she wishes it would "go on and on with her forever," as a "man with keen eyes" studies her.

**Grand Isle**
The Louisiana resort island where the first part of The Awakening takes place. There Edna learns to swim, falls for Robert Lebrun, and meets characters such as the lady in black and the twins in blue. She returns there to drown herself at the end.

**At Fault**
Chopin's first novel (1890), about the widowed Louisiana landowner Thérèse Lafirme. She loves David Hosmer but persuades him to remarry his alcoholic ex-wife Fanny because she believes divorce is wrong.

**Bayou Folk and "Lilacs"**
Bayou Folk (1894) is a collection of Chopin's Louisiana local-color stories, including "Désirée's Baby." Her story "Lilacs" concerns Adrienne, a Parisian singer who yearly visits a convent and drops lilacs at its portico; when she is finally barred from it, the flowers are swept away.

**Katherine O'Flaherty (Creole Louisiana local color)**
Kate Chopin was born Katherine O'Flaherty in St. Louis and lived in Louisiana after marrying Oscar Chopin. Her fiction depicts Creole and Cajun society in New Orleans, Grand Isle, and the Natchitoches area.
